687.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
687.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
687.howItsDone: In Maharashtra, Karnataka and nearby regions, the day after the main Diwali night is kept as Bali Pratipada, honoring King Bali's yearly return; in many places it is also a new-year day and a day of gifts between husbands and wives.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri's tenth day, Ravana burned, Durga sent home, first letters in rice. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Did you begin one small thing? Day six hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: The day after Diwali's Lakshmi night has a guest of its own. In Maharashtra and Karnataka, families light lamps and welcome back a king. Not Rama. A king the gods defeated. In Maharashtra, some say a line that goes, roughly: let troubles go, and let Bali's kingdom come. Bali was a demon king, an asura. So why would anyone light lamps for the return of a demon? Because of how he lost.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE LAKSHMI NIGHT.` → `A KING COMES BACK.` → `A DEMON KING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. Bali, grandson of Prahlad, the boy from the Holi fire, has become so powerful and so generous that he rules all three worlds, and the gods have lost their places. Vishnu comes to restore the balance. He comes as Vamana, a small boy, a young brahmin student with an umbrella and a water pot, to a great sacrifice Bali is holding. Bali is known for never refusing a guest. He tells the boy: ask for anything. The boy asks for three steps of land, measured by his own feet. Bali laughs; ask for more. But Bali's teacher, Shukra, sees through it. He warns Bali: this is Vishnu, and he'll take everything. Bali thinks about it, and gives anyway. I promised, he says, and I won't take back my word. Then the boy grows. With one step he covers the earth, with the second the heavens. There's nowhere left for the third. So Bali bows and offers his own head. Vishnu places his foot there and sends Bali down to a lower realm, Sutala. But the Bhagavata doesn't end it as a punishment. Vishnu praises Bali's truthfulness and promises to stand guard at his door himself. In many tellings, Bali is allowed to come back to the earth once a year to visit his people. In parts of western and southern India, that visit is the day after the Lakshmi night, called Bali Pratipada. So the lamps have one more job: lighting the way home for a king who kept his word when it cost him everything.
screen: `VAMANA: A BOY ASKS FOR THREE STEPS.` · `SHUKRA WARNS; BALI GIVES ANYWAY.` · `THE THIRD STEP ON BALI'S HEAD.` · `BALI PRATIPADA: HIS YEARLY VISIT.` · then, large: `A KING WHO KEPT HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Sit and slow the breath. Bring to mind one promise you made that has grown heavier than you expected: a favor, a visit, a job you said yes to. Don't decide anything yet. Just hold it the way Bali held his word, with the warning in one ear and the promise in the other. Breathe with both. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. In parts of India, the day after the Lakshmi night welcomes back King Bali, who gave three steps of land and kept his word.
screen: `DIWALI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: light the way home. Today, keep one promise that has become inconvenient, and reach out to one person who's drifted away. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: Holi: the festival of colors
688.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
688.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
688.howItsDone: At Holika Dahan, some communities roast ears of new wheat or barley in the bonfire and share them; the next morning, Holi is often a day for visiting, reconciling and starting fresh with neighbors and relatives.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali and King Bali, who kept his word and comes home once a year. Your line was light the way home. Did you keep an inconvenient promise? Day six hundred eighty-eight.
screen: `A KING WHO KEPT HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: At the Holi bonfire, Prahlad walks out of the fire. But the story doesn't stop there, and the Bhagavata Purana carries it further. His father, the king Hiranyakashipu, has tried everything to kill him, and nothing works. Finally, in a rage, he stands in front of his son in the great hall and asks: this Vishnu of yours, who you say is everywhere. Is he in this pillar? The boy says yes. And the king strikes the pillar.
screen: `THE FIRE WAS NOT THE END.` → `IS HE IN THIS PILLAR?` → `THE KING STRIKES IT.`

segments.voice: To understand what happens next, you need the king's boon. Long before, after fierce austerities, Hiranyakashipu had been granted protection, as the Bhagavata tells it, with a long list of conditions. No man or animal could kill him. Not by day or by night. Not inside or outside. Not on the earth or in the sky. Not with any weapon. He thought he'd closed every door. When he strikes the pillar, it splits open, and out comes Narasimha: Vishnu as half man, half lion. Neither man nor animal. He seizes the king at twilight, neither day nor night. On the threshold of the hall, neither inside nor outside. Lays him across his lap, neither earth nor sky. And ends him with his claws, which are not a weapon. Every door the king thought he had closed, opened. Then Narasimha is so terrible in his fury that even the gods are afraid to come near. They send the boy. Prahlad walks up and bows, and Narasimha calms and puts his hand on his head. And when Narasimha offers him any blessing he wants, Prahlad asks for something astonishing: that his father, who tried to kill him again and again, be purified and freed. The Bhagavata says the wish is granted. That's where Prahlad's story ends, and some readers hear in it a key to the morning of colors. The boy who survived everything doesn't ask for revenge. He asks for his father's release. In some villages, people roast ears of the new wheat or barley in the Holi bonfire and share them. A meal of fresh grain, cooked in the fire that ended the cruelty, and eaten together.
screen: `NOT MAN OR BEAST, NOT DAY OR NIGHT.` · `NARASIMHA BURSTS FROM THE PILLAR.` · `ONLY THE BOY CAN CALM HIM.` · `PRAHLAD ASKS FOR HIS FATHER'S RELEASE.` · then, large: `NOT REVENGE, BUT RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring back the small grudge you set on the fire a couple of weeks ago, or a new one. This time, try what Prahlad did, just a little. Not forgiving everything. Just wishing the other person well, once, for one breath: may they be free of whatever made them act that way. Then let it go with the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The fire for Prahlad, Narasimha from the pillar, and a boy who asked not for revenge but for his father's release.
screen: `HOLI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, wish one person well who once wished you ill, even just in your head. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
689.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
689.tomorrow: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
689.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Shiva temples and households divide the night into four watches and bathe the lingam in each, with water, milk, curd, ghee or honey, chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn; Lingodbhava images often appear on the western wall of South Indian Shiva temples.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, Narasimha from the pillar, and Prahlad asking for his father's release. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Did you wish someone well? Day six hundred eighty-nine.
screen: `NOT REVENGE, BUT RELEASE.`

segments.voice: Two gods are arguing about which of them is greater: Brahma, the creator, and Vishnu, the preserver. It's getting heated. And then, between them, a column of fire appears. It has no visible top and no visible bottom. It just goes up and down, beyond seeing. The argument stops. Both of them stare at it. This is one of the best-known stories told about why the lingam is worshiped, and why some people keep Shivaratri awake all night.
screen: `BRAHMA AND VISHNU ARGUE.` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE APPEARS.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, and it's called the Lingodbhava, the appearance of the lingam. The two gods agree: whoever finds an end of the pillar is the greater. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs downward. Brahma becomes a swan and flies upward. They go for ages. Neither finds an end. Vishnu comes back and says honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma, in many tellings, claims he did, and is caught in the lie. Then Shiva appears from inside the pillar of fire. The argument about who's greatest ends with both of them bowing to something with no edges at all. Many Shaivas say Maha Shivaratri is the night that pillar appeared. And that changes how the lingam looks. It's not a statue of a face. It's a sign, a mark, of what can't be measured in either direction. So on Shivaratri, the night is divided into four watches, called praharas, roughly three hours each. In many temples and homes there's an abhisheka in each watch, the lingam bathed again, often with a different offering each time: milk, curd, ghee, honey, and always water. Between, the five syllables: na, mah, shi, va, ya. Om Namah Shivaya. And now our festival weeks are done. Twenty days of the calendar, lamps and colors and threads and cradles and clay and nine nights. Tomorrow the lineage track begins, starting with the path of action, and a short Upanishad read as a whole life.
screen: `LINGODBHAVA: THE PILLAR OF FIRE.` · `NEITHER GOD FINDS AN END.` · `A SIGN OF WHAT CAN'T BE MEASURED.` · `FOUR WATCHES, FOUR BATHS.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and let your attention rest on the breath. Try following one breath all the way in, looking for where it begins. Then all the way out, looking for where it ends. You may not find either edge, the way neither god found the pillar's end. That's fine. When you want to stop, stay three breaths longer, just watching. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept in four watches, and remembered by many as the night the pillar of fire appeared, with no end either way.
screen: `SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, when an argument about who's right starts, stop and notice what's bigger than both of you. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 689 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE ISHA UPANISHAD AS A LIFE.`

690.title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
690.hook: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
690.carry: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
690.tomorrow: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
690.howItsDone: The Isha's opening verse is recited by some Hindus at the start of study or a talk, and teachers of karma yoga often cite it as a posture for working life: act and enjoy without the sense of owning.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and the pillar of fire with no end either way. Your line was stay awake for what matters. Did you notice something bigger than an argument? Today the festival weeks are behind us, and the lineage track begins. Day six hundred ninety.
screen: `A PILLAR WITH NO END.`

segments.voice: Back in year one, you met three roads the tradition describes for a life: karma, the way of action; bhakti, the way of love; jnana, the way of knowing. This week, the end of year two, we take each road for a short walk. First, action. And the text for it is one from year one: the Isha Upanishad, short enough to fit on a postcard. Back then we read it as ideas. This time we read it as a life: how someone who has to work, earn, raise children and pay rent might actually live it.
screen: `THREE ROADS: ACTION, LOVE, KNOWING.` → `FIRST, ACTION.` → `THE ISHA, READ AS A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Karma comes from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. Its plain meaning is action, a deed. The teachings about deeds bearing fruit, and lives following lives, are built around that plain center. On the path of karma, the question isn't how to escape action. It's how to act well. Now the Isha's first verse. In Sanskrit it opens: Isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is to be dwelt in by the Lord, or, in another reading, clothed by the Lord. Then come two short commands. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: enjoy by what is let go, or, as others read it, enjoy what has been given. And: ma gridhah, do not covet. Then a question: kasya svid dhanam. Whose, after all, is wealth? Commentators read the middle line differently. Shankara, the teacher of non-dual Vedanta, hears renunciation in it: give up the sense of owning, and you're free. Others hear something closer to gratitude: take what you're given, as given, and enjoy it without grabbing for more. Both readings meet in the same place. You can live fully in the world, eat, work, enjoy, as long as you don't treat it as yours to hoard. Gandhi is reported to have said that if every other scripture were lost and only this verse survived, Hinduism would still live. For a working life, the verse offers an unusual and practical posture: hold everything you have the way you'd hold something borrowed.
screen: `KARMA: FROM KRI, TO DO.` · `ALL THIS IS DWELT IN BY THE LORD.` · `ENJOY BY LETTING GO. DON'T COVET.` · `WHOSE IS WEALTH?` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIKE SOMETHING BORROWED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest your hands in your lap, palms up. Bring to mind a few things you think of as yours: your phone, your home, your time, your body. One by one, hold each in mind and try the verse's question: whose is this, really? Don't answer in words. Just notice if your grip loosens a little. Then rest with open hands and the breath. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, from the root to do. The Isha's first verse asks you to act and enjoy in a world that isn't yours to own.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life. Today, use one thing you own as if you'd borrowed it, with care and without clutching. Day six hundred ninety.

screen: `DAY 690 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE ISHA UPANISHAD AS A LIFE.`

691.title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
691.hook: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
691.carry: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
691.tomorrow: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
691.howItsDone: Hindus on the path of karma yoga often describe their work, at home, in a job or in service, as an offering done without clinging to its results, and some teachers cite the Isha's second verse alongside the Bhagavad Gita for this.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the Isha's first verse. All this is dwelt in by the Lord; enjoy by letting go; whose is wealth? Did you use something as if you'd borrowed it? Today, the second verse, and the work itself. Day six hundred ninety-one.
screen: `WHOSE IS WEALTH?`

segments.voice: If the first verse of the Isha had stopped at renounce and don't covet, you might expect the next line to say: so leave. Go to the forest. Stop working. It says the opposite. The very next verse tells you to keep doing your work, and to want to live a hundred years doing it. For anyone with a job, a family and a to-do list that never ends, that's a line worth hearing slowly.
screen: `AFTER RENOUNCE, YOU'D EXPECT: LEAVE.` → `IT SAYS: KEEP WORKING.` → `FOR A HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Verse two begins: kurvann eveha karmani, doing works here, indeed. Jijivishet shatam samah, one may wish to live a hundred years. Then the turn. For you, thus, and not otherwise: na karma lipyate nare. Action does not cling to the person. Lipyate is the word for something smeared on, sticking. The picture is of work that doesn't leave a stain. How? Because of the first verse. If you act in a world you don't own, without coveting its results, the action passes through you instead of sticking to you. Shankara reads this verse as a concession for those not yet ready to renounce: if you must act, act this way. Other teachers hear it as a whole path in itself, close to what the Bhagavad Gita teaches about acting without attachment to results. The Gita even uses the same verb for a lotus leaf that water doesn't stick to. Then, a few verses on, the Isha says something sharper. Those who follow avidya, ignorance, or in one reading ritual action alone, enter blinding darkness. Those who delight only in vidya, knowledge, enter a greater darkness still. And whoever knows both together crosses death by the one and reaches the deathless by the other. The commentators argue about exactly what the two words mean here. One common way to hear it: action without understanding is dark, and understanding that refuses to act is darker. Read that way, the Isha asks for both, held at once. So the life the Isha imagines isn't a monk's and isn't a busy person's. It's someone who does a full day's work, wants to keep doing it for a long time, and somehow doesn't get stuck to it.
screen: `DO YOUR WORK; WISH FOR A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `NA KARMA LIPYATE: ACTION DOESN'T CLING.` · `ACTION ALONE, KNOWING ALONE: DARK.` · `BOTH TOGETHER.` · then, large: `WORK THAT LEAVES NO STAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle the breath. Think of one piece of work waiting for you today: a task, a chore, an email. Picture yourself doing it well, fully, with care. Then picture finishing it and setting it down, not checking who noticed, not replaying how it went. Just done, and released. Let the breath move through like water over a lotus leaf. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. The Isha says do your work, wish to live a hundred years doing it, and the action won't cling.
screen: `KARMA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life. Today, do one task completely, then let it go without grabbing at the result. Day six hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 691 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KARMA — THE ISHA UPANISHAD AS A LIFE.`

692.title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
692.hook: the Isha's last verses: a life of work, and at the end, the mind told to remember what was done
692.carry: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life
692.tomorrow: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening
692.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Isha Upanishad whole, beginning and ending with its peace chant, purnam adah. Karma yoga is lived as ordinary work done with care and offered without grasping at its fruit.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-NINETY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the Isha's second verse. Do your work, wish for a hundred years, and the action won't cling. What did you do yesterday without grabbing at the result? Day six hundred ninety-two.
screen: `WORK THAT LEAVES NO STAIN.`

segments.voice: A golden lid. That's the picture the Isha Upanishad reaches for near its end. The face of truth, it says, is covered by a golden disc, and the speaker asks the sun, called here Pushan, the nourisher, to lift it. Then comes a short, startling verse. Let the breath go to the wind. Let this body end in ashes. And then the speaker turns inward, to the mind, and gives it one job. Today, the last of our three days with the Isha: how a life of karma ends.
screen: `A GOLDEN LID ON TRUTH'S FACE.` → `LET THE BODY END IN ASHES.` → `ONE JOB FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: It's the next-to-last verse. In Sanskrit its heart is a short phrase, said twice: kratu smara, krtam smara. Mind, remember. Remember what was done. Said twice, the way you'd repeat something important to someone half asleep. Some translators render kratu as will or resolve rather than mind, but the instruction is the same: remember. Now look at that word, krtam, what was done. It grows from the same root as karma, kr, to do. In the oldest Vedic texts, karma often names the action of the sacrifice, the rite done well. So at the end of the Isha, the mind isn't asked to recite a creed or review its luck. It's asked to look at its karma in the plainest sense: the things this person actually did. Shankara, in his commentary, hears these lines as spoken by someone at the end of a life spent in work and meditation. The final verse is addressed to Agni, the fire, the god who knows all the ways. Lead us by a good path, it asks, keep crooked wrongdoing away from us, and it promises praise. The same verse also appears in the Rig Veda. Put the Isha together and it reads like a whole life. It opens by saying everything is wrapped in the Lord, so enjoy by letting go. In the middle it says to go on doing your work, even for a hundred years. And it closes here, with a body returning to ash, a fire asked for a good road, and a mind asked to remember what it did.
screen: `KRATU SMARA: MIND, REMEMBER.` · `KARMA AND KRTAM: ONE ROOT, TO DO.` · `AGNI, LEAD US BY A GOOD PATH.` · `OPEN, MIDDLE, END: A WHOLE LIFE.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WHAT WAS DONE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Now do what the verse asks, gently. Remember what was done today. Start from waking and walk forward: what you said, what you made, what you carried, whom you helped, what you left undone. Don't grade any of it. Just let each deed pass in front of you, the way a fire lights each thing in a room in turn. When you reach this moment, rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, from the root to do. At the Isha's close the mind is told: remember what was done.

693.howItsDone: Some Hindus, especially in Vaishnava communities, study the Narada Bhakti Sutras in satsang groups, reading a few sutras and a commentary together. Bhakti itself is lived in puja, kirtan, japa and service offered to a chosen form of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the Isha's last verses. The body goes to ash, and the mind is told, twice, remember what was done. Did you name three things you did? Day six hundred ninety-three.
screen: `REMEMBER WHAT WAS DONE.`

segments.voice: In one afternoon you might say you love pizza, love a song, love your grandmother, and love that a meeting got canceled. One word, doing four jobs. Sanskrit has more than one word for love, and a short book attributed to the sage Narada sets out to explain just one of them. It doesn't open with a story or a hymn. It opens like a manual. Now, then, we will explain bhakti. And in its second line it gives the whole definition, almost in a breath.
screen: `ONE WORD, FOUR JOBS.` → `A BOOK THAT OPENS LIKE A MANUAL.` → `NOW, THEN: BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: The Narada Bhakti Sutras are a string of short, packed lines. Nobody knows exactly when they were written; tradition gives them to Narada, the wandering sage with the vina. The first word is atha, now. The Yoga Sutras open the same way, atha, now the teaching of yoga, and so do the Brahma Sutras. It's how a Sanskrit treatise often begins, a door opening. The second sutra is the definition: it is, toward this one, of the form of supreme love. Parama prema. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't name a god in that line. It says asmin, toward this one, and commentators take it as the Lord. The third sutra adds: and it is of the nature of amrita, the nectar of deathlessness. Then the book says what such love does. Having gained it, a person becomes complete, deathless, satisfied. Having gained it, they want nothing, grieve for nothing, hate nothing, and stop scrambling after other pleasures. Knowing it, they become like someone intoxicated, then still, then delighting in the Self. And the word itself? Bhakti comes from the root bhaj, which a standard dictionary gives as to share, to partake, and also to serve and to worship. A devotee is a bhakta. Way back on day four hundred twenty-eight, we saw the word turn up near the end of the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. Here it gets a whole book. And that closes a week that went from lamps and colors and a night awake for Shiva, through three days of karma, to this: love, defined in two words.
screen: `ATHA: NOW. A DOOR OPENS.` · `PARAMA PREMA: SUPREME LOVE.` · `AMRITA: NECTAR, DEATHLESS.` · `BHAJ: TO SHARE, TO SERVE.` · then, large: `IT WANTS NOTHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind what you love most deeply. If you pray, that may be God as you know God. If not, a person, a place, a piece of music. Hold it gently. Then notice what the sutra describes: does wanting quiet down a little? Does the mind go still? You don't need to make anything happen. Just rest near what you love, and watch. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, from bhaj, to share and to serve. The Narada Bhakti Sutras define it as supreme love.

segments.voice: Your line: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening. Today, catch yourself saying love once, and ask which love you mean. Day six hundred ninety-three.
